titre: What a Grave Full of Weapons Does Not Prove
accroche: In 2017, DNA reveals that the Viking warrior of Birka was a woman. The debate did not end there
contenu_vulgarise:
Grave Bj 581, excavated at Birka, Sweden, in the late 19th century, is one of the richest Viking burials ever unearthed. A sword, an axe, a spear, arrows, two shields, two horses, and a board game with its pieces laid out as if for a match.

For more than a century it has been described as the grave of a high-ranking warrior. The description comes down to a single word: *he*.

## What the Genome Settled

In 2017, a Swedish team publishes a genomic analysis of the remains. The result is clear: two X chromosomes, no Y chromosome. The person buried there was biologically a woman.

The news spreads fast, in a simplified form: proof of Viking women warriors, it is said, is now in hand.

The genetic result itself is not disputed. What is disputed is what can be concluded from it.

## Two Objections, and They Are Not of the Same Kind

The first concerns the bones. The 1878 excavations were not conducted to today's standards, and the museum's collections have been reorganized several times since. Critics asked whether the bones analyzed really came from this grave. The team responded by documenting the chain of custody; the objection has largely subsided.

The second is more interesting, because it targets the reasoning rather than the sample.

A grave is not a résumé. Grave goods are deposited by the living, and they can signify rank, lineage, an inheritance, a symbolic function, a family's claim. Not necessarily the occupation of the deceased. No one argues that a child buried with a sword wielded one.

The argument deserves to be taken seriously. But it has an awkward property: it was made with this insistence only once the individual's sex had been established. For a century, the same weapons in the same grave had been enough to conclude “warrior.”

## The Shift

This is where the case becomes exemplary, and it is so for all funerary archaeology.

If grave goods do not prove function, then they did not prove it before 2017 either, and a share of the “warrior graves” recorded over the past century rests on an inference that has just been declared insufficient.

If grave goods do prove function, then Bj 581 is indeed the burial of a female fighter.

What cannot be done is to apply the strict rule only to the cases that disturb. The genome did not merely change the reading of one grave: it made visible a criterion thought to be objective that was not applied in the same way depending on what one expected to find.

repere.texte: The 2017 genomic analysis yields two X chromosomes and no Y. Grave Bj 581, described as that of a warrior ever since its excavation in 1878, held a woman.
repere.source: Hedenstierna-Jonson et al., “A female Viking warrior confirmed by genomics,” American Journal of Physical Anthropology, 164, 2017

carte.punch: For a century, the weapons were enough to say “warrior.” Then came the DNA.
carte.idee: Viking grave Bj 581, one of the best-armed at Birka, held a woman. The debate then shifted: do grave goods prove an occupation? They did not prove one any more before her sex was known.

quiz.question: What did the 2017 genomic result mainly bring to light?
choix: That a criterion held to be objective was not applied in the same way from case to case
That 19th-century excavations had mixed up bones from several graves
That women commonly fought in Viking Age armies
That Viking grave goods were deposited with no connection to the deceased
quiz.explication: Biological sex is established and little disputed. What the affair reveals is that the inference “weapons, therefore warrior,” held to be obvious for a century, was subjected to scrutiny only once the result was unexpected. A single grave says nothing about how common female fighters were, and grave goods are not therefore arbitrary. They are simply ambiguous.

choix: A polished bronze mirror, a sign of wealth

quiz_supplementaire.question: How did the team respond to the objection about the provenance of the bones analyzed?
choix: By declining to comment, judging the question baseless
By documenting the chain of custody of the bones since the excavation
By carrying out a complete new excavation of the Birka site
By publishing a partial retraction of the 2017 study
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Faced with doubts about a possible mix-up between collections after the museum's reorganizations, the team documented the chain of custody of the bones, which largely put an end to the objection.
